supersedes.reason: Replace named AgentMux examples in the unstarted current plan with a generic authorized external client or embedding host while preserving the same ctxmux-owned artifact boundary.

tasks.title: Define Run-scoped client-authorized artifact ingress
tasks.objective: Freeze the smallest host-local capability, ownership, retry, resource, and lifecycle contract for explicitly supplied opaque bytes beside one live native Run.
tasks.outcome: Clients can reason about authorization, Run scope, operation disposition, and cleanup without introducing source policy, application semantics, remote deployment, Backend fallback, or a second context identity into ctxmux.
acceptance: A reviewed ADR defines ArtifactId, exact target RunId, logical-name handling, RunHostPath or reference semantics, capability discovery, operation key, committed or failed or unknown disposition, lease, release, TTL, Run-terminal cleanup, and daemon-start cleanup.

The caller alone decides whether clipboard, drag-and-drop, file, generated, or other bytes may be shared; ctxmux never reads or infers source policy and daemon limits cannot be disabled by caller authorization.

Placement is daemon-host local: ctxmux chooses the physical destination beside the target Run and does not deploy over SSH, accept a client destination, transfer across Runs or hosts, or expose a remote-filesystem abstraction.
Artifact stage, ordinary Run input, and release remain separate operations with separate correlated outcomes; no stage receipt claims that the Run or an application consumed the bytes.

The trust boundary covers same-UID exposure, path safety, permissions, quotas, misleading names, partial upload, disconnect, response loss, conflicting operation-key reuse, terminal-state Run, unsupported Backend, and restart cleanup.
No Agent identity, message, permission, media decoding, prompt, UI, or workspace policy enters foundational protocol types.

verification.proves: Owner, host locality, retry disposition, capability, resource, security, lifecycle, and non-goal boundaries are reviewed before implementation.
Architecture links, wrong-case mappings, and ordinary repository gates pass.

tasks.title: Implement bounded idempotent native-Run staging
tasks.objective: Implement the approved public protocol and daemon owner with bounded streaming, operation-status recovery, atomic exact-byte publication, and race-safe cleanup for live native Runs.
tasks.outcome: A public client can recover a lost commit response without duplicate files, while every known failure publishes nothing and every committed artifact remains bounded and attributable to one Run.
acceptance: The Rust protocol SSOT defines capability, begin, chunk, commit, status, and release frames, bounded identities, declared length and digest, and generated TypeScript parity without placing a multi-megabyte artifact in one NDJSON frame or creating a general transaction bus.

The same operation key with identical RunId and content converges on one receipt; conflicting reuse fails. A lost success response is queryable during the documented daemon epoch, and SDKs do not retransmit uncertain bytes blindly.

The daemon validates a live native Run before consuming chunks, chooses an owner-only directory and create-new temporary file, rejects client destinations and unsafe names, verifies exact length and digest, and atomically publishes before success.
Per-upload, per-Run, concurrent, and aggregate quotas bound memory, disk, descriptors, and tasks; slow upload backpressure cannot starve status, cancellation, release, stop, or shutdown.

Pre-commit cancellation, malformed frames, timeout, disconnect, digest mismatch, and quota failure leave no ArtifactId, file, descriptor, task, or charge. Commit, release, TTL or eviction, Run-terminal cleanup, and startup cleanup share one lease-aware owner policy.
Exited, interrupted, or missing Runs, imported tmux Runs, unsupported Backends, and capability mismatch reject before bytes or filesystem mutation; artifacts never migrate to a new RunId.

verification.proves: Protocol generation, TypeScript parity, operation idempotency, response loss, parser bounds, filesystem atomicity, quotas, cleanup, and Run lifecycle regressions pass.
Upload, status, commit, release, retry lifetime, capability, and unsupported semantics match the implementation.

tasks.title: Expose public artifact composition without host policy
tasks.objective: Expose staging, status, input composition, and release to clean Rust, TypeScript, and CLI consumers while keeping source authorization, transport deployment, and application UX in embedding hosts.
tasks.outcome: Any authorized external client can use one public boundary on the host of the ctxmuxd it reaches, with no private daemon access, client-selected destination, or media-specific API.
acceptance: Rust and @ctxmux/sdk expose streamed file or bytes, operation status, committed ArtifactId and RunHostPath or reference, cancellation, release, and typed errors with bounded buffering through the public protocol only.

The CLI offers an explicit file-to-live-Run staging command with size, digest, identity, target Run, materialized reference, and lifetime; it never reads source state or uploads merely because attach starts.

A composition helper may stage then send the reference through correlated input, but stage, input, and release results remain distinct so unknown input is not replayed and commit truth is not rewritten.

Documentation states that the receiving ctxmuxd stages on its own host. An external host may connect through separately owned authenticated transport, but ctxmux owns no SSH installation, credentials, or connection policy in this Feature.

A clean TypeScript consumer stages caller-authorized media bytes and arbitrary fragmented binary data, sends the path to a shell Run, and proves the exact digest; a denial fixture issues no request and creates no file.
Examples contain no named product, Agent, clipboard, Electron, React, conversation, or permission API and do not bypass Backend capability checks.

verification.proves: Rust, CLI, TypeScript, clean-consumer, exact-byte, denial, stage or input separation, and repository regressions pass.
Generic composition, host locality, caller-owned policy, receipts, limits, cleanup, and unsupported behavior are documented.

tasks.title: Qualify artifact ingress under hostile lifecycle and load
tasks.objective: Prove the complete public artifact contract under adversarial bytes, filesystem races, uncertain responses, disconnects, Run replacement, quotas, cleanup, restarts, concurrency, and resource pressure.
tasks.outcome: Artifact ingress has no silent partial publication, duplicate commit, leaked file, resource escape, unsafe retry, cross-Run reuse, unsupported fallback, or media-specific shortcut.
acceptance: Deterministic tests cover every frame boundary, arbitrary bytes, invalid metadata, traversal and symlink attempts, duplicate or conflicting operation keys, length or digest mismatch, late frames, cancellation, timeout, disconnect before or after commit, status query, and release races.

Real filesystem fixtures prove private modes, atomic visibility, exact bytes, no partial reads or orphan temporaries, lease-safe release, TTL or quota eviction, Run-terminal cleanup, and startup cleanup on every supported local platform.

Stress lanes cover many Runs and uploads, slow or silent clients, aggregate exhaustion, shutdown, and repeated cancellation with bounded RSS, descriptors, tasks, disk, and latency and no control-path starvation.
A Run replacement fixture proves an artifact never crosses RunId; the new Run stages independently. Imported tmux, terminal-state, and unknown-capability targets fail before upload.
Security review confirms no source reads, client physical destination, hidden remote transport, path disclosure through unrelated Runs, or stronger same-UID isolation claim.
Clean public-boundary qualification and documentation contain no silent fallback; unknown operation disposition remains explicit when its documented query lifetime is unavailable.

verification.proves: Protocol, lifecycle, chaos, stress, security, resource, cleanup, SDK, CLI, and clean-consumer lanes pass together.
Every invariant, platform, resource result, unsupported capability, and residual risk is auditable.
